anti_patterns: Connecting the sidecar to a single relay with no alternative: one censoring, slow, or offline relay decides every slot's outcome
Blind-signing headers without checking relay reputation and relay-monitor data: the proposer is bound by its signature while the body is still escrowed
Running without a local-build fallback (no min-bid floor): a relay outage turns into missed slots instead of lower-value local blocks
Builders submitting full payloads to unvetted relays: a malicious relay can frontrun or leak the builder's orderflow
Treating relay inclusion as censorship-resistance: a compliant or dominant builder set can still exclude transactions, only diversity mitigates this
Registering a wrong or exchange-controlled fee-recipient address: bids pay the registered address and cannot be redirected after signing
avoid_when: No trust in any third-party relay is acceptable: the pattern inherently delegates pre-signature validity and data-availability trust to relays
The chain has no builder market or relay infrastructure: there is no external auction to source blocks from
The operator requires enshrined in-protocol PBS guarantees: this is the interim trusted-relay design, not the final protocol change
Slot-timing margins cannot absorb the extra getHeader/submitBlindedBlock round trip within the slot window
Regulatory or policy constraints forbid outsourcing block construction to external builders
best_practices: Connect mev-boost to multiple reputable relays so one censoring or degraded relay cannot decide the slot
Set a min-bid floor so the consensus client falls back to local block production when no bid clears it
Monitor relay behavior continuously with a relay monitor (bid value delivered, validity, latency) and disconnect underperformers via circuit breakers
Register the correct fee-recipient address before proposal duties so builder payments land where expected
Keep the sidecar pinned to the latest Builder API release supported by the consensus client
Prefer relays that simulate builder submissions and publish auditable activity data
benefits: Democratized MEV revenue: solo and small validators earn competitive builder bids instead of only base priority fees, estimated at over 60% higher staking rewards
Role specialization: validators propose and attest while capitalized builders run MEV search, ordering optimization, and low-latency infrastructure
Pre-signature validity filtering: relays simulate builder payloads and forward only the highest valid bid header, shielding proposers from invalid blocks and spam
Censorship-resistance through competition: validators choose any number of relays and builders compete openly, so orderflow has many paths to inclusion
Deployable without consensus changes: a consensus-client sidecar implementing the Builder API, compatible with all major clients, ahead of enshrined PBS
component_types: MEV-Boost Sidecar: validator-side relay aggregator that queries configured relays, selects the most valuable valid header, and returns the unblinded payload after signing
Relay: doubly-trusted auctioneer and escrow that simulates builder blocks, verifies fee-recipient payment, forwards only the top bid header, and releases the body after the proposer's signature
Block Builder: specialized bidder that aggregates mempool transactions and searcher bundles, orders them for maximum value, and submits full payloads plus bids to relays
Consensus and Validator Client: blockspace seller that registers fee-recipient, blind-signs the winning header, and proposes the released block to the network
Relay Monitor: public auditor that scores relay behavior and performance from on-chain data so validators can prune dishonest or degraded relays
context: On proof-of-stake Ethereum the validator selected to propose a slot must produce a full execution block, but building the most valuable block requires MEV search, private orderflow access, and latency-optimized infrastructure. Validators that build locally earn only standard priority fees while MEV-capable operators out-earn them, which centralizes stake toward sophisticated pools and exposes users to predatory ordering. MEV-Boost implements out-of-protocol proposer-builder separation: the validator runs a sidecar that sells its slot's blockspace in a sealed-bid auction. Builders submit full blocks with a fee payment to relays, relays simulate and aggregate them and forward only the most valuable valid block header, the proposer blind-signs that header, and the relay then releases the full body for proposal. Equivocation slashing binds the proposer to its signed header, so the builder can reveal the body safely.
design_principles: Separate Proposing from Building: consensus voting stays with validators while transaction ordering moves to a competitive builder market
Blind Commitment: the proposer commits to a header without seeing the body (commit-reveal), enforced by slashing on equivocation
Auction for Blockspace: each slot is a sealed-bid first-price auction where the highest valid bid wins inclusion
Explicit Trust with Auditability: relays are named trusted parties whose simulation, payment verification, and liveness are publicly monitored
Safe Fallback: local block production remains available when no external bid clears the validator's minimum

technology_stack: mev-boost sidecar wired into the consensus client (Lighthouse, Lodestar, Nimbus, Prysm, Teku)
Ethereum Builder API specification (ethereum/builder-specs) endpoints: registerValidator, getHeader, submitBlindedBlock
MEV-Boost relays (e.g. Flashbots boost-relay) running API, housekeeper, and website components
Builder multiplexers (mev-boost, mev-rs, commit-boost) for relay aggregation and min-bid fallback
Relay monitors and dashboards (mevboost.pics, relay monitor) for bid and liveness auditing
tradeoffs: Trusted-relay risk: relays see full builder blocks and bid values, so they can censor, delay, or leak orderflow; mitigation is relay diversity and public monitoring, not cryptography
Builder centralization persists: the auction isolates MEV economies of scale at the builder layer but a dominant builder can still extract rent or censor
Slot-timing pressure: the getHeader/sign/submitBlindedBlock round trip must fit the ~12 second slot, so relay and network latency directly bound liveness
Relay liveness dependency: a relay outage or degraded simulation pipeline means missed high-value bids unless local-build fallback is configured
Operational complexity: an extra sidecar process, relay allowlist, fee-recipient registration, and API version tracking on top of the normal three-client stack
Weaker trust model than enshrined PBS: out-of-protocol separation relies on reputation and escrow rather than protocol-enforced guarantees
use_cases: Solo validators outsourcing block construction to earn builder-market bids without running MEV infrastructure
Staking pools connecting one mev-boost instance to multiple relays to maximize per-slot revenue across many validators
Builders competing in a sealed-bid auction by aggregating searcher bundles and optimizing transaction ordering
Operators setting a min-bid floor so the consensus client falls back to local building when external bids are too low
Ecosystem watchers auditing relay neutrality and performance with relay monitors and public dashboards
